<reason>Side A (CON) wins decisively on both the neurobiological threshold for suffering and the practical ethics of research regulation. Biologically, Side A dismantled Side B's core premise that rudimentary learning equals subjective valence, showing that isolated spinal cords and basic algorithms adapt to feedback without feeling distress, whereas protected non-mammals (like fish and cephalopods) possess nociceptors and integrated affective homologs that a dish-grown cortical cluster lacks. Strategically, Side A turned the animal review framework's 3Rs against Side B: under pressure questioning, Side B conceded that the "Reduction" pillar would require rationing the number of organoids created just like live mice, while offering only "stable culture conditions" as concrete protection. Side A proved this adds zero meaningful protection to painless cell cultures while destroying the high-throughput screening scalability that allows organoids to replace live, genuinely sentient mammals.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In Rebuttal 2 [A4.3-A4.6], Side A capitalized on Side B's concession [B4.3] that animal review would require reducing the number of organoids grown "just as we reduce the number of mice," demonstrating that rationing high-throughput cell cultures sabotages the 3Rs' Replacement pillar and prolongs reliance on live lab animals.</best_rebuttal>
